overview: The file consists of two State Department docket or “list of papers” sheets summarizing correspondence about exporting arms, munitions, and explosive-related materials to Japanese-controlled Dairen in Manchuria. The first records a September 1930 request by Jardine, Matheson & Co. Ltd. to ship nitration toluol through Dairen for use at the Mukden Arsenal and the Department’s explanation of the permit procedure. The second summarizes June–July 1935 correspondence with Dayton, Price & Co. concerning whether an export license was required for a shipment of sporting arms or munitions to Dairen.

people.name: D. H. Wardell
people.role: Representative of Jardine, Matheson & Co. Ltd.

subfiles.title: Docket sheet on shipment of nitration toluol to Dairen
subfiles.about: This docket sheet records correspondence concerning permission to ship nitration toluol to Dairen for use by the Mukden Arsenal.
subfiles.summary: Jardine, Matheson & Co. Ltd., through D. H. Wardell, requested a permit and procedural information for shipping nitration toluol to Dairen, Manchuria, for use at the Mukden Arsenal. A State Department reply dated September 19 explained the applicable procedure and enclosed two blank permit applications.

subfiles.title: List of papers on Dayton, Price & Co. shipment to Dairen
subfiles.about: This sheet lists four items of correspondence about the licensing of a Dayton, Price & Co. shipment of sporting arms or munitions to Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The sheet summarizes correspondence exchanged from June 27 through July 16, apparently in 1935, between Dayton, Price & Co. and the State Department. R. W. Brown submitted or supported an application relating to a shipment for sporting purposes, after which the Department advised that an export license for Dairen was unnecessary. The company subsequently asked when a response could be expected, and the Department referred it back to its July 3 letter.

interest: These sheets provide a compact record of how the State Department handled private commercial requests to export strategically sensitive goods to Japanese-controlled Manchuria before the Second Sino-Japanese War. Particularly useful is the juxtaposition of an explosive precursor destined for the Mukden Arsenal in 1930 with a sporting-arms shipment in 1935, including the Department’s conclusion that an export license was unnecessary in the latter case. The documents also preserve corporate representatives’ names, office-routing symbols, dates, and references to permit forms that could guide researchers to related correspondence or regulatory files.
